---
title: "Patient Similarity Networks"
description: "Representing patients as networks of pairwise similarity, for finding subgroups and predicting outcomes."
---

Papers on the patient similarity network (PSN) approach. Each data type, or
each feature, becomes a network whose nodes are patients and whose edge weights
say how similar two patients are. The networks are then used to find patient
subgroups or to predict outcomes.

## Pai & Bader (2018): Patient similarity networks for precision medicine

Pai S, Bader GD. Patient similarity networks for precision medicine. *Journal
of Molecular Biology* 430(18 Pt A), 2924–2938 (2018).

- [doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2018.05.037](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2018.05.037)
- [Free full text on PubMed Central (PMC6097926)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6097926/)
- [PDF in lab-papers](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/lab-papers/blob/main/pai-2018-patient-similarity-networks.pdf)
  (lab members only)

**Why read it.** A short review that introduces the PSN approach and makes the
case for it. Any data type can be turned into a network once you define a
similarity measure, so very different data end up in the same form. A patient
missing from one network can still be in the others. Results read as "this
patient resembles these patients", which is close to how clinicians reason, and
networks can be shared without sharing the raw data. It covers the two PSN
methods available at the time: [SNF](similarity-network-fusion.qmd) for
clustering and netDx for classification.

**Focus on.** The section "Patient similarity networks as a framework for
clinical prediction", up to and including the clustering subsection. It gives
the arguments for PSNs and a plain-language description of SNF. Read the netDx
subsection if your project predicts a known outcome (classification) rather than
discovering subgroups. The closing section on challenges (scaling to large
cohorts, tuning parameters, using prior biological knowledge) is a useful list
of open methods problems. The introduction on clinical risk models is
background you can skim.

## Gliozzo et al. (2022): Heterogeneous data integration methods for patient similarity networks

Gliozzo J, Mesiti M, Notaro M, Petrini A, Patak A, Puertas-Gallardo A,
Paccanaro A, Valentini G, Casiraghi E. Heterogeneous data integration methods
for patient similarity networks. *Briefings in Bioinformatics* 23(4), bbac207
(2022).

- [doi:10.1093/bib/bbac207](https://doi.org/10.1093/bib/bbac207)
- [Free full text on PubMed Central (PMC9294435)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9294435/)
- [PDF in lab-papers](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/lab-papers/blob/main/gliozzo-2022-psn-data-integration-methods.pdf)
  (lab members only)

**Why read it.** A broader and more recent survey than Pai & Bader. It covers
both steps of the work: building a PSN from one data type, including which
similarity measure suits which kind of data, and integrating several data
types. It sorts integration methods into three groups:

- **PSN-fusion:** build one PSN per data type, then fuse them into a single
  network. SNF and its variants are here, along with multiple kernel learning
  methods and netDx.
- **Input data-fusion:** combine the data types into one dataset first, for
  example with PCA-, CCA- or matrix factorisation-based methods such as MOFA+,
  then build a single PSN.
- **Output-fusion:** analyse one PSN per data type separately, then combine the
  results.

**Focus on.** The "PSN construction" section and Tables 1–2, which list the
similarity measures used for each data type. For continuous data the authors
suggest the scaled exponential kernel of Euclidean distance, which is what SNF
uses; for categorical data, chi-squared distances; for mixed clinical data, one
option is to compute a similarity per variable and average them. Then read
"SNF-based methods" and Table 4, which list SNF variants such as ANF (designed
to be cheaper to compute than SNF) with whether code is available and in which
language. The Discussion covers open problems: missing data, scaling to large
cohorts, and the lack of common benchmarks for comparing methods. The input
data-fusion and output-fusion sections are a reference for when you compare SNF
against other approaches.
